category_title: Students with learning disabilities who equate high-volume note-taking with learning and use abbreviations to increase speed
minimal_context: Ben is taking notes on strategic note-taking paper during a 15-minute video lecture on Electro-Plasma Rockets to capture facts for future study.
dialogue:
TUTOR: We are going to watch this 15-minute video lecture on Electro-Plasma Rockets. Please use your strategic note-taking paper to take notes while it plays.

STUDENT: Okay. I want to write down as many points as possible. Main points means facts, so I want to write more to learn off of.

TUTOR: Alright, I am starting the video now. Just do your best to take notes.

STUDENT: (Writing quickly) I'm using abbreviations to increase my speed so I can record more lecture points. When you write a lot of notes down, you feel good about yourself.

TUTOR: The video is moving to the next section. How are your notes coming along?

STUDENT: It's going too fast! I decided to work as fast as I can and write the words down that I wanted because the more work the better, but I'm struggling a great deal with writing fast enough. Forget about three to six main points, I want to put more than you’re supposed to do, but I can't keep up with the lecture!

options.A: Ignore all undesirable behaviors exhibited by the student as he attempts to take notes during the video lecture.
options.B: Provide a structured note-taking paper for the video lecture with specific boxes for Topic, Background Knowledge, 3-6 Main Points, and Vocabulary.
options.C: Deliver verbal statements or gestures (e.g., high five, thumbs up) indicating approval beyond simple acknowledgment of his notes.
options.D: Approach the situation from an affective lens. Share a personal experience of being gifted, discuss its benefits, and ask if he is satisfied with not utilizing his gift.
